title: Mike Joyce (musician) - Wikipedia
notes: Michael Adrian Paul Joyce, born 1 June 1963, Manchester, to Irish Catholic parents; the Smiths' drummer from October 1982 to 1987. Before them the Hoax (Manchester) and the Belfast punk band Victim. After: Sinéad O'Connor with Andy Rourke; Morrissey's Interesting Drug and The Last of the Famous International Playboys (1989); Suede, Buzzcocks, Public Image Ltd, Julian Cope, P. P. Arnold, Pete Wylie in the 1990s. Won his 1996 royalties case against Morrissey and Marr. Memoir, The Drums, November 2025. Cites a MusicRadar interview (March 2018) headed with his words: 'I had three styles of playing: fast and loud, faster and louder and fastest and loudest. The Smiths was a shock'.

title: The Smiths - Wikipedia
notes: The band (Morrissey, Johnny Marr, Andy Rourke, Mike Joyce), Manchester, 1982-1987: 'a back-to-basics guitar, bass and drums sound'. Simon Wolstencroft drummed on the first demos but would not join; Joyce joined after auditions. Craig Gannon on second guitar in 1986.

title: This Charming Man - Wikipedia
notes: Single, 31 October 1983, produced by John Porter. 'The rhythm section of Andy Rourke and Mike Joyce provides a beat more danceable than usual for a Smiths track. The drums were originally programmed on a Linn LM-1, under the direction of producer John Porter. Porter used the programme to trigger the sampled sounds of the live drum kit'.

title: How Soon Is Now? - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded July 1984 at Jam Studios, London, with John Porter. 'To make sure the beat was the same throughout the song, Porter used a Drawmer noise gate triggered by 16th note cowbell hits coming from his LinnDrum.' The rhythm compared to Bo Diddley's Mona; Joyce on the red light bulbs in the studio.

title: The Queen Is Dead (song) - Wikipedia
notes: 'Mike Joyce's layered drum intro was the result of a looped sample that Joyce recorded.' Stephen Street: 'We had this very antiquated sampler ... We got Mike to play this rumbling rhythm and then sampled a small section of it.' Live, 'Joyce reproducing the song's artificial drum intro live without tapes'.

title: Barbarism Begins at Home - Wikipedia
notes: Meat Is Murder (1985): 'a funk-influenced track built around Andy Rourke's repetitive bassline and Marr's Chic-influenced guitar riffing'; Joyce: 'The bass line's a killer.' A live favourite.

title: Far Out Meets: The Smiths' Mike Joyce discusses Morrissey, Marr and modern music (Jordan Potter)
notes: 28 September 2022. 'I went to see Buzzcocks play in Manchester when I was about 14-15, and that was it ... the first gig that I'd seen where I was completely transfixed by John Maher and his playing ... he had a red kit ... his cymbals were all flat playing cymbals'. On the Smiths: 'I don't really sit on a groove with a lot of them'; his pick, How Soon Is Now?, 'just for the groove'; 'I just played drums for what I thought worked for the track'. Names Donald Johnson of A Certain Ratio among Manchester's finest drummers.

title: He bangs the drum (Hotpress)
notes: 11 February 2008. 'The main thing for a drummer is to listen to the music ... a great drum fill is only great if it sounds right within the song'; 'a lot of drummers tend to be too flamboyant for their own good'; on Charlie Watts: 'he's an amazing drummer, every Stones track that has ever been just sounds fantastic'.

title: Mike Joyce's 10 best drum tracks with The Smiths (Radio X)
notes: 19 November 2025: The Queen Is Dead's 'unrelenting rhythm'; Barbarism Begins at Home, 'Mike Joyce rises to the challenge admirably'; Panic 'given extra heft by Mike Joyce's powerful drum work'; London's last seconds in double time; Death of a Disco Dancer 'one of Joyce's greatest "feel" performances'.
